\title{Measuring and Decomposing Latency\\
       in a Closed-Loop EEG Music System}
\author{Kirthan Kulkarni}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Several closed-loop systems that continuously adapt music to a user's electroencephalogram
(EEG) have been implemented in the past, yet none of the systems that we could examine
reports a measured end-to-end latency, even though neurofeedback studies find that feedback
effects weaken at a 0.5--1 second latency. We present a closed-loop EEG music system which
utilizes consumer hardware, and measure its latency component by component. The system
estimates arousal using a frontal $\log(\beta/\alpha)$ index, maps it onto a nine-level
prompt ladder following the iso-principle, and plays audio from a library of pre-rendered
MusicGen segments. Music generation runs $1.05$--$6.27\times$ slower than real time in
every configuration that was tested, which motivates the precomputed library setup.
Employing a precomputed library reduces worst-case audio latency from $8.0$~s to $1.0$~s.
The deployed end-to-end latency is $6.5$~s, of which $84.6\%$ is attributable to the
analysis path rather than the generative model. Evaluated on labelled eyes-open/eyes-closed
transitions from 109 subjects of a public EEG dataset, the deployed estimator is worse than
all 9 alternative configurations on both detection latency and information rate, and the
same holds on Muse~2 recordings with real, unspliced transitions from 13 subjects. The
architecture shows an analysis-path floor of $0.189$~s and end-to-end latency of $0.439$~s,
at which information rate is $1.50\times$ that of the deployed configuration. On the Muse,
however, eye closure barely changed alpha at AF7 and AF8, the channels the index is computed
from ($1.06\times$, $p = 0.11$), while TP9 and TP10 showed a clear rise ($1.82\times$). We also
report
four statistical properties of closed-loop EEG data that are relevant to study design. All
EEG results use public datasets or synthetic signals, and all 77 quantitative claims are
regenerated by a single Python script. No claim of therapeutic efficacy is made.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} closed-loop systems $\cdot$ EEG $\cdot$ latency $\cdot$
neurofeedback $\cdot$ music generation $\cdot$ reproducibility

% =============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Music listening is a non-invasive way to influence a user's affective state, and recent
research seeks to make it adaptive by closing the loop through the user's brain activity.
Such systems record EEG continuously and estimate an affective state from it. The music
changes in response. Several of these systems have
been built and described~\cite{mindmelody,mindtomusic,ehrlich,neurophone,minimalist}, and
this area has already been reviewed~\cite{dashagres}.

These systems are typically described as real-time, but the time they take to respond has
not been studied much. In neurofeedback, delay is itself an experimental variable:
Belinskaia et
al.~\cite{belinskaia} trained parietal alpha with feedback delayed by 0, 250 and 500~ms and
found that sustained post-training change was negatively correlated with latency and absent
at 500~ms. Asai et al.~\cite{asai} compared feedback delays of 0, 1 and 20~s and found that
the trained EEG microstate increased significantly only when feedback was not delayed.

In this work, we build a closed-loop EEG-based music system on consumer hardware (Muse~2)
and analyze its latency. The system consists of a four-channel Muse headband, a frontal
arousal index normalised to each listener's baseline, a controller that applies the
iso-principle over a nine-level prompt ladder, and an audio engine that selects from a
library of pre-rendered segments rather than generating music online. We decompose the
end-to-end delay into its analysis and audio components. Alternative estimator
configurations are then evaluated against labelled ground truth to find the lowest latency
the architecture can reach.

Our contributions are summarised as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item We report a measured latency budget for a closed-loop EEG music
        system, and show that most of the delay ($84.6\%$ of $6.5$~s) comes from
        processing the EEG signal rather than generating the music.
  \item On public EEG from 109 subjects, and again on Muse~2 recordings from 13
        subjects, we show that the deployed estimator is worse
        than all 9 alternatives on both detection latency and information rate, and that
        the system's latency floor ($0.439$~s end-to-end) is $1.50\times$ as informative as
        the deployed setting.
  \item We demonstrate that, for a controller with a finite prompt space, a precomputed
        audio library is preferable to online generation independently of generator
        speed, and reduces worst-case audio latency by a factor of 8.
  \item We identify four statistical properties of closed-loop EEG data that affect the
        design and analysis of studies using such systems, and calibrate one of them
        against synthetic ground truth.
  \item We find that on the Muse~2 itself the frontal channels carry little eye-state
        alpha, which bears on any system that builds an index from them.
\end{enumerate}

% =============================================================================
\section{Related Works}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Closed-Loop EEG Music Systems}

Recent systems differ widely in how they decode affect and how they produce music.
MindMelody decodes valence and arousal with a Transformer-GNN encoder and plans
interventions with a retrieval-augmented language model, then conditions MusicGen-medium on
the result~\cite{mindmelody}. It reports $76.8\%$ accuracy for valence and $72.4\%$ for
arousal across subjects on DEAP. Ran et al.\ generate emotional music in real-time from
EEG~\cite{mindtomusic}. Ehrlich et al.\ demonstrate a closed-loop system with synthesised,
affective music~\cite{ehrlich}. Velasquez-Pe\~na et al.\ control Ableton Live via a
consumer-grade Muse~S headband~\cite{neurophone}, while Monroy-D'Croz et al.\ design a
minimal interface driven by prefrontal EEG, using the Lab Streaming
Layer~\cite{minimalist}. In each case, EEG is used to shape the music, and most of these
systems decode affect with more sophistication than the single index used here. We make no
claims to better decoding performance than these methods.

None of these works report a measured latency from when the signal is obtained to audio output.
MindMelody reports neither latency nor inference time, and does not specify its hardware.
Monroy-D'Croz et al.\ state a 4~s sliding window with 0.5~s updates but report no latency
and no control condition. Ehrlich et al.\ come closest. Their feedback loop uses a 4~s
analysis window at $87.5\%$ overlap (0.5~s step), with zero-phase filtering chosen to avoid
delaying the signal, and they tuned their feedback parameter to match the subjective
impression of latency. They do not report an end-to-end value.

\subsection{Feedback Latency}

Delay is treated as a primary variable in neurofeedback~\cite{belinskaia,asai} and as a
design requirement in interactive music generation; Gesture2Music, for example, reports
25--30~ms inference latency against the 100~ms threshold commonly regarded as acceptable
for real-time interaction~\cite{gesture2music}. We apply the same standard to EEG-driven music.

\subsection{The Iso-Principle}

The iso-principle holds that music should first match a listener's present state and then
lead it gradually toward a target~\cite{altshuler}. Its supporting evidence comes largely
from fixed, non-adaptive sequences: Starcke et al.\ randomised 107 participants to four
pre-set sequences after a sadness induction. Group differences after listening were
significant for positive affect and valence ($\eta^2 = 0.08$ and $0.09$), with the iso
sequence scoring highest, although not significantly above a sequence of two happy
pieces~\cite{starcke}. The sequences were fixed in advance and did not respond to the
listener. However, a larger, pre-registered study did not replicate this advantage:
Lowe-Brown et al.\ randomised 193 participants after an anxiety induction to iso,
compensatory or unguided playlists built from their own songs. They found no significant
difference between iso and compensatory listening, although exploratory analyses showed
greater increases in calmness after either guided playlist than after unguided
listening~\cite{lowebrown}. The evidence for the iso-principle is therefore mixed. We
return to the implications of this in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}.

% =============================================================================
\section{System Design}
\label{sec:system}

\subsection{Overview}

The system forms a loop of four stages: acquisition, arousal estimation, prompt selection
and audio rendering. A Muse~2 headband streams four EEG channels at 256~Hz over Lab
Streaming Layer. An arousal index is computed over sliding windows, normalised to the
listener's baseline, and mapped by the controller to one of nine text prompts. The audio
engine plays segments associated with the current prompt and crossfades to a new segment
when the prompt changes.

\subsection{Arousal Estimation}

The frontal channels AF7 and AF8 are averaged. Each window of length $W$ is detrended,
band-pass filtered between 1 and 45~Hz, notch filtered at 60~Hz, and transformed with
Welch's method~\cite{welch} to obtain band powers $P_\alpha$ and $P_\beta$. The raw index
\begin{equation}
  I_t = \log \frac{P_\beta(t)}{P_\alpha(t)}
\end{equation}
is computed every hop $H$ and smoothed with a one-pole filter of time constant $\tau$:
\begin{equation}
  s_t = (1-a)\,s_{t-1} + a\,I_t, \qquad a = 1 - e^{-H/\tau}.
\end{equation}
The smoothed index is standardised against a 120~s eyes-open baseline with mean $\mu_b$
and standard deviation $\sigma_b$:
\begin{equation}
  z_t = \frac{s_t - \mu_b}{\sigma_b}.
\end{equation}
Windows exceeding a 350~$\mu$V peak-to-peak amplitude are rejected and do not update the
smoother. The deployed configuration uses $W = 4$~s, $H = 1$~s and $\tau = 3$~s.

\subsection{Prompt Controller}

The controller quantises $z_t$ onto a ladder of nine rungs, each spanning 0.5 standard
deviations and centred on rung $c = 4$:
\begin{equation}
  k_t = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(c + \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{z_t}{w}\right),
        \,0,\,8\right), \qquad w = 0.5.
\end{equation}
Following the iso-principle, the controller does not move directly to the target rung
$k^\ast$, obtained by applying the same mapping to the target $z^\ast$, but plays the rung
adjacent to the listener's current rung in the direction of the target:
\begin{equation}
  \hat{k}_t =
  \begin{cases}
    k^\ast, & |z_t - z^\ast| \le \delta, \\
    k_t + \operatorname{sgn}(k^\ast - k_t), & \text{otherwise,}
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
where $\delta = 0.35$ is a deadband within which the listener is considered to be at the
target. For relaxation, $z^\ast = -1$.
Each rung corresponds to one text prompt, so the controller's output space consists of
exactly nine strings. A minimum dwell time $D$ prevents a new prompt change until $D$
seconds have elapsed since the previous one.

\subsection{Audio Engine}

Each of the nine prompts has 32 pre-rendered 8~s segments, generated offline with
MusicGen~\cite{musicgen}, for a total of 288 segments (38.4 minutes). When the prompt
changes, the current segment is abandoned and the engine performs an equal-power crossfade
of duration $T_{\mathrm{xf}}$ into a segment from the new rung.

Two properties motivate this design. The controller emits only nine distinct prompts, so a
library covers its entire output space exactly, and re-synthesising one of nine prompts
online would be redundant even with an arbitrarily fast generator. Latency is the other
reason. A streaming generator must play each queued segment to completion, so its audio
latency is bounded by the queue rather than by generation speed:
\begin{equation}
  L_{\mathrm{audio}}^{\mathrm{stream}} \le Q\,S, \qquad
  L_{\mathrm{audio}}^{\mathrm{library}} \le T_{\mathrm{xf}},
\end{equation}
where $Q$ is the queue depth and $S$ the segment duration. In our configuration this
reduces the worst-case audio latency from 8.0~s to 1.0~s.

% =============================================================================
\section{Latency Characterisation}
\label{sec:latency}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}

\paragraph{Generation benchmark.} We measured MusicGen throughput in nine benchmark runs
spanning two GPU tiers (a laptop GPU and a datacenter NVIDIA T4), two inference backends
(Hugging Face Transformers and Audiocraft) and three precision modes (fp32, fp16 with
autocast, and fp16 with half-precision weights), giving 44 configuration cells.

\paragraph{Ground truth for the analysis path.} No EEG was recorded for this paper.
Estimator configurations were evaluated on the PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery
Dataset~\cite{schalk,physionet}, loaded with MNE-Python~\cite{mne}. Each of its 109
subjects has a one-minute eyes-open and a one-minute eyes-closed resting run, recorded at
160~Hz with a 64-channel cap. The dataset includes AF7 and AF8, the channels of the
arousal index. It has no TP9 or TP10, so the nearest temporal sites, T9 and T10, stand in
for them. For each subject we joined eyes-open 0--30~s, eyes-closed 0--60~s and eyes-open
30--60~s into a 120~s session with one rising and one falling transition. Segments were
mean-centred and crossfaded over 50~ms so that the join adds no step. A spliced transition
is instantaneous, while a real eye closure takes time to raise alpha, so the measured
detection latencies are upper bounds on the estimator alone. We also generated 50 synthetic
sessions at the Muse's 256~Hz, each with six alternating 60~s blocks of 1/$f$ background
and an alpha component whose power steps by a factor of 1.34 at every block boundary. All
estimators were run through the deployed feature extractor at the dataset's own sampling
rate.

\paragraph{Muse 2 recordings.} To check the result on the system's own hardware, we also
used the public HEROIC dataset~\cite{heroic}, in which participants wore a Muse~2 at home or
in the lab. Every session begins with about 61~s of eyes closed, a spoken cue, and about
61~s of eyes open, recorded continuously at 256~Hz. The transition is therefore real rather
than spliced, and the measured latency includes each participant's reaction to the cue,
whose onset we take as the transition time. Two rules were fixed before any estimator was
run. Four recordings appear twice in the archive under different subject folders, so each
was kept once and the two folders were treated as one subject. Recordings with any gap
longer than 0.5~s inside the eye blocks were excluded, and shorter jitter was interpolated
onto a uniform grid. This left 36 of 61 unique recordings, from 13 subjects. Subjects
contribute between one and five sessions, so each subject is summarised by the median over
their own sessions, and we report medians across subjects.

\subsection{Metrics}

The analysis-path latency of a windowed estimator is the sum of the window centroid delay,
the mean hop quantisation delay and the smoother's group delay:
\begin{equation}
  L_{\mathrm{analysis}} = \frac{W}{2} + \frac{H}{2} + \tau,
  \qquad L_{\mathrm{total}} = L_{\mathrm{analysis}} + L_{\mathrm{audio}} .
  \label{eq:budget}
\end{equation}
\emph{Detection latency} is the time from a labelled transition to the first point at
which the estimator crosses the midpoint between the two state means and stays across it
for at least 0.5~s. A crossing that is undone sooner is counted as noise. Without this rule
the noisiest estimators would be credited with chance crossings. For windowed estimators,
whose outputs arrive every 0.5 or 1~s, the rule changes nothing; it matters only for the
streaming ones. Each configuration is scored per subject and summarised by the median
across subjects. Discriminability $d$ is the standardised difference in the estimator's
output between eyes-closed and eyes-open data at least 8~s from a transition. Because
consecutive outputs are autocorrelated, we also compute the number of independent
observations per minute,
\begin{equation}
  n_{\mathrm{ind}} = \frac{60}{H}\cdot\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho},
  \label{eq:nind}
\end{equation}
where $\rho$ is the lag-1 autocorrelation of the output on a 1~s grid. We score each
configuration by its information rate
\begin{equation}
  R = d\,\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{ind}}},
  \label{eq:info}
\end{equation}
the $t$-statistic per square-root minute, which governs how precisely a session of fixed
duration resolves a difference in state. Latency alone would favour no smoothing, and
discriminability alone would favour smoothing everything to a constant; $R$ balances the
two.

\subsection{Generation Throughput}

Every one of the 44 configuration cells ran between $1.05\times$ and $6.27\times$ slower
than realtime, with the best case on the datacenter T4. The bottleneck is the sequential
autoregressive decode loop rather than arithmetic throughput: on the T4, fp32 outperformed
fp16 with half-precision weights by a factor of $0.952$, and the ordering
fp32~$<$~fp16-half~$<$~fp16 held in 6 of 6 cells. Autocast inserts a type conversion at
every operation, a cost that is amortised in large batched training workloads but not in
batch-1 decoding. Between-run variation for an identical configuration reached $1.96\times$
on the thermally limited laptop and $1.18\times$ on the T4, so single-run measurements on
consumer GPUs should be reported as ranges.

\subsection{End-to-End Latency Budget}

Table~\ref{tab:budget} decomposes the deployed latency. The analysis path contributes
$5.5$~s, comprising $2.0$~s of window centroid delay, $0.5$~s of hop quantisation and
$3.0$~s of smoother group delay. With a $1.0$~s crossfade, the worst-case end-to-end
latency is $6.5$~s, of which $84.6\%$ is analysis. Against the PhysioNet transitions the
deployed estimator's median detection latency is $4.50$~s. This is shorter than the budget
for a simple reason. A midpoint crossing needs the smoother to cover half of a step, which
takes $\tau \ln 2 = 2.08$~s rather than $\tau$, so the expected crossing time is
$W/2 + H/2 + \tau\ln 2 = 4.58$~s.

\begin{table}[h]

\label{tab:budget}
\begin{tabular}{lr}

component & latency (s) \\
\midrule
window centroid ($W/2$, $W = 4$~s) & 2.0 \\
hop quantisation ($H/2$, $H = 1$~s) & 0.5 \\
smoother group delay ($\tau = 3$~s) & 3.0 \\
\textbf{analysis path} & \textbf{5.5} \\

\textbf{end-to-end} & \textbf{6.5} \\

\end{table}

\subsection{Estimator Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:estimators} compares the deployed estimator with two representative
alternatives, and Figure~\ref{fig:tradeoff} shows all ten configurations. On the medians
across 109 subjects, all nine alternatives are both faster and more informative than the
deployed setting. The deployed setting is therefore not a latency--accuracy trade-off. It
lies off the efficient frontier. The result does not depend on the scoring rule or the
data: it is also 9 of 9 under the first-crossing rule, on T9/T10, and on the 50 synthetic
sessions. Medians can hide individual subjects, so we also counted them. The retuned
windowed configuration beat the deployed one on both axes in $78.5\%$ of subjects.

windowed ($W = 2$~s, $H = 0.5$~s, $\tau = 0.5$~s) & 1.50 & 1.35 & 10.9 & 4.68 \\

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{public-estimator-tradeoff.png}
\caption{Detection latency against information rate $R$ for each estimator configuration,

\label{fig:tradeoff}
\end{figure}

The principal cause is the smoother. At $\tau = 3$~s, consecutive outputs are nearly
identical ($\rho = 0.972$), yielding only $0.9$ independent observations per minute. The
smoother is therefore simultaneously the largest latency term and the main source of the
autocorrelation discussed in Section~\ref{sec:stats}; reducing $\tau$ improves both.

\subsection{Confirmation on Muse Hardware}

On the HEROIC recordings the deployed estimator was again beaten on both axes by all 9
alternatives, on subject medians and on session medians alike (Figure~\ref{fig:muse},
right). This comparison uses TP9/TP10, because at AF7/AF8 the eye-state contrast is too small
to act as ground truth (Section~\ref{sec:validation}). The deployed estimator took a median of
$8.49$~s to register eye opening. That is longer than on PhysioNet, as it should be: a real
transition adds the participant's reaction to the cue and the time alpha takes to fade. The
retuned windowed configuration beat the deployed one on both axes in $82.9\%$ of sessions,
and the floor's information rate was $2.68\times$ the deployed value. Real transitions and
dry electrodes leave the conclusion of this section unchanged.

\subsection{Latency Floor}

A causal streaming estimator has no window centroid or hop quantisation, so its only
delays are filter group delay and smoothing. A second-order design with $\tau = 0.1$~s
reaches an analysis-path latency of $0.189$~s. Table~\ref{tab:floor} combines
analysis-path and crossfade durations and compares each total with the 500~ms delay at
which Belinskaia et al.~\cite{belinskaia} no longer observed a training effect.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{End-to-end latency by configuration, relative to the 500~ms delay of Belinskaia
et al.}
\label{tab:floor}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
analysis path (s) & crossfade (s) & end-to-end (s) & ratio to 500~ms \\
\midrule
deployed, 5.500 & 1.00 & 6.500 & 13.0 \\
retuned, 1.750 & 1.00 & 2.750 & 5.5 \\
floor, 0.189 & 1.00 & 1.189 & 2.4 \\
floor, 0.189 & 0.25 & 0.439 & 0.9 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

At the floor, the crossfade becomes the largest term, so the dominance of the analysis
path is a property of the configuration rather than of the architecture. Moving to the
floor does not lower the information rate. Per-window discriminability falls from
$d = 2.07$ to $0.39$, but the number of independent observations rises from $0.9$ to
$49.7$ per minute, and the information rate is $1.50\times$ that of the deployed
configuration. The floor is not the most informative setting, though. That is the retuned
windowed configuration, at $R = 4.68$, which trades about a second of extra latency for
it.

These results have limits. Detection latency does not keep falling with the budget: at the
floor the median is $0.63$~s, and below $\tau = 0.1$~s it rises again, because the output
becomes noisy enough that crossings no longer hold for 0.5~s. Under the first-crossing rule
the same estimators appear to detect in 0.10--0.16~s, which is the flattery the hold rule
exists to remove. The eyes-open/eyes-closed contrast is also considerably larger than the
contrast expected between adaptive and non-adaptive music. No session has been run at
these settings, so the floor is characterised offline rather than in deployment.

\subsection{Controller Stability at Low Latency}

Adopting a faster estimator also requires changes to the controller. We drove the real
controller with $z$ series reconstructed from 66 PhysioNet sessions, every one with enough
clean eyes-open windows to form a baseline (132 minutes in total). Through the
$W = 2$~s, $H = 0.5$~s, $\tau = 0.5$~s configuration, 4176 of 6986 prompt changes arrived
before the preceding crossfade had completed, or 31.7 per minute. At the deployed settings
there were none. A less smoothed index crosses rung boundaries frequently. Imposing a
minimum dwell $D \ge T_{\mathrm{xf}}$ guarantees that no change begins before the previous
crossfade ends, and reduces the count to 0 on both the PhysioNet and the synthetic
sessions. The dwell adds to worst-case latency, which becomes
$L_{\mathrm{analysis}} + D + T_{\mathrm{xf}}$.

% =============================================================================
\section{Statistical Properties of Closed-Loop EEG Data}
\label{sec:stats}

\subsection{Autocorrelation}

Across 99 unspliced PhysioNet resting runs with no rejected windows, the deployed index on
AF7/AF8 has a median lag-1 autocorrelation of $\rho = 0.918$. The 40 one-minute DEAP trials
of participant~1 give the same value on AF3/AF4 ($\rho = 0.918$). For a 20-minute session
at a 1~s hop, the AR(1) effective sample size
\begin{equation}
  N_{\mathrm{eff}} = N\cdot\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}
  \label{eq:neff}
\end{equation}
is $51.0$ of $1200$ windows. A test that treats the windows as independent therefore
overstates its test statistic by $\sqrt{1200/51.0} = 4.85\times$. The Muse recordings agree:
within each clean 61~s eye block the same index gives $\rho = 0.905$, an overstatement of
$4.47\times$. Figure~\ref{fig:acf}
shows that the index falls below $1/e$ within 4~s, a time scale set largely by the
smoother rather than by the listener. One-minute runs contain none of the slow drift of a
longer session, so these values are lower bounds on the autocorrelation a closed-loop
session would show.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth]{public-autocorrelation.png}
\caption{Autocorrelation of the deployed arousal index as a function of lag, across 99
PhysioNet resting runs (AF7/AF8).}
\label{fig:acf}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Continuous Audio-Neural Coupling}

Cross-correlating the audio envelope with the neural index over a full session loses
statistical power precisely when the intervention succeeds. A listener who reaches the
target and remains there holds the controller on a single rung, leaving little
controller-driven variation in the audio to correlate. The estimator itself is sound: it
recovers a known 6~s lag exactly from synthetic data. The limitation therefore lies in the
outcome measure, not in the estimator.

\subsection{Event-Locked Responses}

Restricting analysis to moments when the rung changes restores power. It also introduces a
confound: a rung change occurs because $z$ has moved, and $z$ continues to move afterward,
so a positive event-locked effect arises even when the music has no influence. We
calibrated this confound using synthetic sessions with known ground truth. The estimator
returned $+1.503$ for a simulated responder, $-1.467$ for an anti-responder and $+0.011$ for
an unrelated session. A fourth session, constructed with no audio effect but with rung
changes triggered by boundary crossings as in the real controller, returned $+0.435$. Its
pre-onset slope ($+0.0573$~z/s, against $+0.0012$ for a genuine response) identifies it as
triggered rather than caused. A positive within-condition event-locked effect is therefore
not evidence of an effect; only the contrast against a yoked sham condition is
interpretable.

\subsection{Dichotomised Outcomes}

Time spent within a target band is clinically interpretable but discards information about
distance from the band and saturates for listeners far outside it. We simulated crossover
studies with 10 participants, using the PhysioNet autocorrelation and within-session
spread. Mean $z$ reached 80\% power at an effect of 0.13 standard deviations; time in band
needed 1.06, roughly eight times larger. We therefore designate mean $z$ as the primary
outcome. We do not derive a required sample size from these simulations, because
one-minute resting runs understate the within-session variance of a 20-minute session.

% =============================================================================
\section{Signal Validation}
\label{sec:validation}

We assess two separate properties: whether the index channels record cortical activity,
and whether the $\log(\beta/\alpha)$ index tracks arousal.

\paragraph{Cortical signal.} On the PhysioNet resting runs, using the deployed extractor
and 350~$\mu$V rejection threshold, alpha power on AF7/AF8 rose by a median of $1.80\times$
from eyes open to eyes closed (Figure~\ref{fig:alpha}). It rose in $86.8\%$ of the 91
subjects with enough clean windows (Wilcoxon $p = 3.2 \times 10^{-12}$, $d_z = 0.96$),
with a median of $19.8\%$ of windows rejected. On T9/T10 the rise was
smaller, $1.46\times$, but it occurred in $89.0\%$ of all 109 subjects
($p = 1.2 \times 10^{-17}$). A rise in band power does not by itself show an alpha
rhythm, so we also measured the eyes-closed increase in spectral peak prominence. The
median was $1.35\times$ on AF7 and $1.41\times$ on AF8, above a $1.2\times$ criterion. The
frontal channels of this dataset therefore show a distinct alpha peak on eye closure. They
were recorded with a gel cap, and dry consumer electrodes at the same sites may not.

\paragraph{Muse hardware.} On a Muse, they largely do not. In the HEROIC recordings, alpha
at AF7/AF8 rose by a median of only $1.06\times$ on eye closure, in 9 of 13 subjects
(Wilcoxon $p = 0.11$), and the alpha peak barely changed (prominence ratios of 1.08 at AF7
and 1.03 at AF8). At TP9/TP10 the same sessions show a clear effect of $1.82\times$, in 10 of
13 subjects ($p = 0.021$; Figure~\ref{fig:muse}, left). The Muse references its electrodes
to Fpz, close to AF7 and AF8, and alpha shared by the reference and the frontal sites would
cancel in the difference. We have not tested that explanation. Whatever its cause, the
arousal index is computed from the two channels where, on this hardware, one of the most robust
effects in EEG is barely visible. This does not show that the index carries no information
about arousal, which is a different and smaller signal, but it removes the evidence that
those channels record cortical activity reliably on a Muse.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{public-heroic-muse.png}
\caption{Muse~2 recordings from the HEROIC dataset (13 subjects). Left: alpha power around
the cue to open the eyes, normalised to each session's eyes-closed mean; lines are medians
across sessions and bands interquartile ranges. Right: detection latency against
information rate on TP9/TP10, subject medians; the shaded region contains configurations
that improve on the deployed setting on both axes.}
\label{fig:muse}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{public-alpha-validation.png}
\caption{Alpha power through the PhysioNet eyes-open and eyes-closed runs, normalised to
each subject's eyes-open mean. Lines are medians across subjects and bands interquartile
ranges. Left: AF7/AF8, from which the arousal index is computed. Right: T9/T10, the
dataset's nearest sites to the Muse's TP9/TP10.}
\label{fig:alpha}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Arousal.} We tested the index on the public DEAP dataset~\cite{deap}, which
pairs 32-channel EEG with self-reported affect, using the same feature extractor as the
live system. On AF3/AF4 the index correlated with reported arousal at $\rho = +0.303$
($p = 0.058$) and with valence at $+0.082$. The direction of the arousal correlation was
positive across 7 of 7 independent montages (sign test $p = 0.016$). Because the Muse
results above favour TP9/TP10, we also computed the index from the DEAP sites around them,
averaging T7, P7, T8 and P8. It correlated with arousal at $\rho = +0.454$ ($p = 0.003$).
That is not evidence that the temporal sites are better. Averaging four frontal channels
(AF3, AF4, Fp1, Fp2) also raised the correlation, to $+0.342$, a neighbouring temporoparietal
set (CP5, CP6, P7, P8) gave $+0.295$, and nine channel sets were tried on 40 trials from one
participant. What the comparison does suggest is that moving the index to TP9/TP10 need not
cost it sensitivity to arousal.

% =============================================================================
\section{Reproducibility}
\label{sec:repro}

Every quantitative claim in this paper is regenerated by a single script, which compares
each recomputed value with the value stated here and fails on any disagreement; all 77
claims currently reproduce. The claims draw on these sources only: the generation
benchmarks, the system's own configuration, synthetic sessions with known ground truth, and
the public PhysioNet, HEROIC and DEAP datasets. The script reads stored results by default and
regenerates them from the raw public data on request. Recordings made during the system's
development are not used for any claim. Detection scoring was fixed before the public
results were computed, and the first-crossing rule is reported beside it as a sensitivity
check.

% =============================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

This work makes no claim that the intervention benefits listeners. No participants were
enrolled, no EEG was recorded for this paper, and no adaptive/sham comparison exists.

\paragraph{Latency relative to the neurofeedback literature.} The deployed latency is
$13\times$ the delay at which Belinskaia et al.\ no longer observed an effect, and the
retuned configuration remains $5.5\times$ that delay. These findings concern operant
neurofeedback, in which the listener must perceive a contingency, whereas the mechanism
proposed here is the iso-principle, whose evidence comes from fixed sequences without any
contingency~\cite{starcke}. If a fixed iso sequence is effective, then an adaptive system
must outperform a fixed playlist, not silence. A yoked sham condition provides that
comparison. The pre-registered evidence that a fixed iso sequence is effective at all
remains mixed~\cite{lowebrown}, so an adaptive system cannot rely on the iso literature for
its plausibility either.

\paragraph{Controller degeneracy.} A controller can operate correctly yet produce no
manipulation. If its rungs are wide relative to the spread of $z$, a listener can occupy a
single rung for an entire session, and a yoked sham would then be acoustically identical to
the adaptive condition. We recommend that studies of adaptive audio report the number of
prompt changes and distinct prompts per session.

\paragraph{Data and scope.} The PhysioNet results come from a 64-channel gel cap sampled at
160~Hz. The Muse recordings confirm the estimator comparison on the target hardware, but
only at TP9/TP10, from 13 subjects in a single protocol. On those recordings the index
channels showed almost no eye-state alpha, so the arousal index itself is weakly supported
on the hardware it is built for. Computing it from TP9/TP10, or re-referencing, are
alternatives we have not evaluated. The PhysioNet transitions are spliced and therefore
instantaneous, T9/T10 stand in for TP9/TP10 in that dataset, and its resting runs last one
minute, which limits the autocorrelation and power estimates of Section~\ref{sec:stats}.

% =============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a closed-loop EEG-driven music system and a measured decomposition of its
end-to-end latency. Contrary to the common emphasis on faster generative models, the
dominant source of delay was the analysis path. That dominance is a property of the
configuration rather than the architecture. On public data from 109 subjects, the deployed
estimator was dominated by all 9 alternatives on both latency and information rate, the
same held on Muse~2 recordings with real transitions, and the architecture's floor of $0.439$~s end-to-end was $1.50\times$ as informative as the
deployed setting. On the Muse, however, the frontal channels from which the index is
computed responded little to eye closure, and a future version of the system should
address that. We also described four statistical properties of closed-loop EEG data
that should inform the design of studies using such systems. These results characterise
the system's engineering behaviour. Establishing whether adaptive music confers any benefit
over a fixed playlist requires a controlled study with participants, which remains future
work.

% =============================================================================
\section*{Code and Data Availability}

All code is available at
\url{https://github.com/kirthankulkarni-bit/Brain-Music-Therapy}. The 77 claims are checked
by \texttt{python scripts/verify\_claims.py}, which regenerates the public-data results
with \texttt{--recompute}, and the figures are drawn by
\texttt{scripts/make\_public\_figures.py}. The PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Dataset
is openly available from PhysioNet and is downloaded by the scripts on first use. HEROIC is
openly available from Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.11493897, CC BY 4.0) and must be
downloaded by hand; \texttt{scripts/public\_data.py} describes where to put it. DEAP is
available from its authors on request and is not redistributed. The audio library is
omitted for size; its manifest is included and \texttt{scripts/build\_library.py}
regenerates it.
